# Space-Time Symmetries in Scalar Quantum Field Theory on Static Space-Times

This study investigates the structure and implementation of space-time symmetries in scalar quantum field theory, with particular attention to the challenges posed by interacting theories, formulated on static space-time backgrounds. The central goal is to understand how the geometric symmetries of a given manifold—encoded in its isometry group—can be consistently realized as symmetries of the associated quantum theory, both in the free and interacting cases.

The analysis begins in the Euclidean setting, where the quantum field theory is defined on a static Riemannian manifold. This choice of starting point is motivated by the relative analytical simplicity of Euclidean field theories, which often admit more tractable mathematical descriptions than their Lorentzian counterparts, particularly when interactions are present. Working in this framework, we examine the structure of the isometry group of the underlying Riemannian manifold, with the aim of understanding how its symmetries manifest at the level of the quantum theory.

A key structural result is that the isometry group of the static Riemannian manifold can be generated by one-parameter subgroups, each of which admits a well-defined quantization as either a self-adjoint semigroup or a unitary group acting on the quantum field theory's Hilbert space. This dichotomy reflects the distinct roles played by different types of isometries: transformations associated with, for instance, time translations are naturally implemented as self-adjoint (contraction) semigroups, reminiscent of Euclidean time evolution, while spatial isometries are represented unitarily, preserving the inner product structure directly.

Building on this classification, the self-adjoint semigroups associated with the relevant one-parameter subgroups are analytically continued to yield one-parameter unitary groups. This analytic continuation procedure is the crucial technical step that bridges the Euclidean and Lorentzian formulations of the theory: by continuing the parameter labeling the semigroup into the complex plane and restricting to purely imaginary values, one recovers a genuine unitary evolution appropriate to a Lorentzian signature. Through this construction, the full isometry group of the original Euclidean manifold is shown to give rise to a unitary representation of the isometry group of the corresponding Lorentzian manifold, thereby establishing a rigorous correspondence between the symmetries of the Euclidean and Lorentzian quantum field theories.

To illustrate the generality and applicability of this method, the construction is explicitly worked out in the example of hyperbolic space. In this case, the Euclidean manifold is hyperbolic space itself, whose isometry group is well understood, while its Lorentzian continuation is identified with Anti-de Sitter space. This example serves as a concrete and physically significant test case, demonstrating how the abstract framework developed here can be applied to a space-time of direct interest in mathematical physics, and providing explicit unitary representations of the Anti-de Sitter isometry group derived from the underlying Euclidean structure.

# Space-Time Symmetries in Scalar Quantum Field Theory on Static Space-Times

## Introduction and Motivation

The relationship between Euclidean and Lorentzian formulations of quantum field theory has long occupied a central place in mathematical physics, both for its foundational significance and its practical utility in constructive approaches to quantum field theory. While the Wick rotation—the formal replacement of time by imaginary time—provides a powerful heuristic tool for connecting the two formulations, establishing this connection on a rigorous mathematical footing, particularly in the presence of curved backgrounds, presents substantial technical challenges. This is especially true when one wishes to track not merely the field theory itself but also its symmetry structure across the continuation from Euclidean to Lorentzian signature.

This study addresses precisely this issue: the systematic and rigorous treatment of space-time symmetries in scalar quantum field theory defined on static space-times, with particular attention to how the isometry group of the underlying geometry manifests itself at the level of the quantum theory before and after analytic continuation.

## Euclidean Quantum Field Theory on Static Riemannian Manifolds

The analysis begins on the Euclidean side, where the theory is formulated on a static Riemannian manifold. Such manifolds possess a distinguished structure: a one-parameter group of isometries corresponding to translations in the Euclidean time direction, together with additional spatial isometries reflecting the symmetries of the underlying static slice. The full isometry group of the manifold can be decomposed, at least locally, into one-parameter subgroups, each of which acts on the space of quantum fields (or more precisely, on the associated Hilbert space of the Euclidean theory) through a specific type of operator.

A central technical result of this work is the demonstration that each one-parameter subgroup of isometries is quantized either as a **self-adjoint semigroup** or as a **unitary one-parameter group**, depending on the geometric character of the corresponding Killing vector field. Isometries associated with directions that behave, roughly speaking, like "Euclidean time"—directions along which the metric is positive-definite and translations correspond to a contraction or dissipative structure—are naturally represented by self-adjoint (typically positivity-preserving or contraction) semigroups, analogous to the role played by the Euclidean time-translation semigroup generated by the Hamiltonian in more standard treatments of Euclidean field theory. Isometries corresponding to "genuinely spatial" directions, by contrast, are represented unitarily, since these symmetries do not involve any element of Euclidean time evolution and therefore do not carry the analytic structure necessary for a semigroup interpretation.

This dichotomy—self-adjoint semigroups for time-like Euclidean directions versus unitary groups for spatial directions—is not merely a convenient classification but reflects a deep structural feature of Euclidean quantum field theory, closely related to the reflection positivity and analyticity properties that underlie the Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction theorem. By carefully identifying which generators of the isometry algebra fall into each category, the present approach lays the groundwork for a systematic continuation procedure.

## Analytic Continuation to Unitary Representations

The heart of the construction lies in the analytic continuation of the self-adjoint semigroups identified in the Euclidean theory into unitary one-parameter groups. This step mirrors, at the level of representation theory, the analytic continuation that relates Euclidean Green's functions to Wightman functions in flat-space quantum field theory. Here, however, the continuation is performed not merely on correlation functions but directly at the level of the operators implementing the isometries, allowing one to track the full symmetry content of the theory through the continuation process.

Concretely, each self-adjoint semigroup, generated by some non-negative self-adjoint operator, admits an analytic continuation in its parameter from real (Euclidean time) values to imaginary (Lorentzian time) values. Under suitable conditions—chiefly, that the semigroup extends to a strongly continuous unitary group upon this continuation—one obtains a bona fide unitary representation of the corresponding one-parameter subgroup of the *Lorentzian* isometry group. Combined with the unitary representations already established for the purely spatial isometries (which require no continuation, since they act identically in both signatures), this procedure yields a full unitary representation of the entire isometry group of the Lorentzian manifold obtained by continuing the original Euclidean space-time.

This result is significant because it shows that the symmetry structure of the Lorentzian quantum field theory can be derived entirely from Euclidean data, without the need for an independent construction of the Lorentzian theory. In particular, it demonstrates that the analytic continuation procedure preserves not only the dynamics (encoded in the two-point functions or path integral measure) but also the full group-theoretic symmetry content of the theory.

## Illustrative Example: Hyperbolic Space and Anti-de Sitter Space

To demonstrate the practical applicability and internal consistency of this framework, the paper works through the explicit example of **Euclidean Anti-de Sitter space**, realized as hyperbolic space, and its continuation to **Lorentzian Anti-de Sitter space**. Hyperbolic space serves as a particularly instructive test case: its isometry group is well understood, given by the pseudo-orthogonal group $O(d,1)$ acting on the hyperboloid model, and its continuation to Lorentzian Anti-de Sitter space—with isometry group $O(d-1,2)$—is a well-studied example in both the mathematical and physical literature, not least due to its relevance to the AdS/CFT correspondence.

By explicitly identifying the relevant one-parameter subgroups of the hyperbolic isometry group, classifying them according to the self-adjoint/unitary dichotomy described above, and performing the analytic continuation explicitly, the paper verifies that the resulting unitary representation correctly reproduces the known unitary representations of the Anti-de Sitter isometry group acting on the Lorentzian quantum field theory. This example thus serves both as a consistency check on the general formalism and as a concrete illustration of how abstract representation-theoretic machinery translates into calculable results in a physically relevant setting.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these results establish a rigorous and generally applicable framework for connecting Euclidean and Lorentzian quantum field theories on static space-times, with particular emphasis on the fate of space-time symmetries under the Euclidean-to-Lorentzian continuation. By carefully distinguishing self-adjoint from unitary quantizations of the isometry generators on the Euclidean side, and by providing an explicit continuation procedure that upgrades self-adjoint semigroups to unitary groups, the paper offers a mathematically precise account of how the full isometry group of a Lorentzian space-time can be recovered from Euclidean data. The worked example of hyperbolic space continuing to Anti-de Sitter space further underscores the utility of this approach, suggesting promising avenues for extending the analysis to more general classes of static and stationary space-times of interest in both mathematical physics and quantum gravity.

# Geometries Beyond the Familiar: Euclidean, Riemannian, and Lorentzian

Geometry, at its core, is the study of shape, space, and the relationships between points, lines, and curves. While most people's intuitive understanding of geometry stems from the flat, predictable world described by **Euclidean geometry**, mathematicians and physicists have developed far richer frameworks to describe more complex realities—namely, **Riemannian** and **Lorentzian geometry**.

## Euclidean Geometry: The Foundation

Named after the ancient Greek mathematician Euclid, this is the geometry we learn in school. It describes flat space governed by familiar axioms: parallel lines never meet, the angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees, and the shortest distance between two points is a straight line. The Pythagorean theorem, distance formulas, and basic trigonometry all operate within this Euclidean framework. For centuries, it was considered the only "true" geometry, an absolute description of physical space.

## Riemannian Geometry: Embracing Curvature

In the 19th century, Bernhard Riemann generalized geometric thinking to include curved spaces. **Riemannian geometry** allows for spaces where the rules of Euclidean geometry no longer hold—think of the surface of a sphere, where triangles can have angle sums greater than 180 degrees, and "straight lines" become great circles. 

The key mathematical tool here is the *metric tensor*, which defines how distances and angles are measured at every point in a space, even as that space curves and twists. Crucially, Riemannian geometry deals with **positive-definite metrics**, meaning distances are always positive and space behaves consistently in every direction, even if that space is curved. This framework proved essential for understanding the geometry of surfaces, manifolds, and eventually the fabric of the universe itself.

## Lorentzian Geometry: The Geometry of Spacetime

**Lorentzian geometry**, named after Hendrik Lorentz, takes a further conceptual leap. It emerged from the need to describe the universe not just in three spatial dimensions, but in four-dimensional **spacetime**, as required by Einstein's theory of relativity. 

The crucial distinction is that Lorentzian metrics are **not positive-definite**—they have mixed signature, typically written as (-,+,+,+) or (+,-,-,-). This means that the "distance" between events in spacetime (called the *interval*) can be positive, negative, or zero, corresponding respectively to spacelike, timelike, and lightlike (null) separations. This structure encodes the physical reality that time behaves fundamentally differently from space, and it allows Lorentzian geometry to describe phenomena like time dilation, the light cone structure of causality, and the curvature of spacetime around massive objects, as in general relativity.

## A Continuum of Geometric Thought

These three geometries form a conceptual progression: Euclidean geometry describes flat space, Riemannian geometry generalizes this to curved spaces while preserving a consistent notion of positive distance, and Lorentzian geometry further generalizes the concept to include the indefinite signature necessary for modeling time and causality. Together, they represent one of mathematics' most profound achievements—the ability to rigorously describe not just the space we intuitively perceive, but the curved, dynamic, and even time-inclusive structures that underlie our modern understanding of the physical universe.

# Abstract

We present a general construction of unitary representations of the isometry group of a static spacetime on the one-particle Hilbert space of a free scalar quantum field theory, obtained via analytic continuation from the associated Euclidean theory. Starting from a static Lorentzian spacetime with isometry group $G$, we consider the Wick-rotated Euclidean manifold, on which the time translation subgroup is compactified to a circle, and construct the Euclidean Green's function using the heat kernel of the elliptic operator governing the theory. The reflection positivity of the Euclidean two-point function, together with the Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction theorem, allows us to recover the Lorentzian Wightman function and the corresponding one-particle Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ as a Hilbert space completion of a suitable space of Euclidean data. We show that the action of the isometry group $G$, realized geometrically on the Euclidean section, extends to a strongly continuous unitary representation on $\mathcal{H}$, with the Hamiltonian (generator of time translations) automatically implemented as a positive self-adjoint operator, reflecting the underlying reflection positivity structure. This construction bypasses the need for an a priori canonical quantization or choice of vacuum state, instead deriving the Hilbert space and its unitary $G$-action directly from Euclidean correlation functions. We illustrate the method with explicit examples, including the static patch of de Sitter space, the Rindler wedge, and asymptotically flat static black hole backgrounds, showing how the resulting representations reproduce the expected thermal (KMS) and boundary properties of the corresponding Lorentzian vacua. The approach clarifies the group-theoretic origin of thermality in these backgrounds and provides a rigorous, representation-theoretic framework for constructing physically sensible vacua in static curved spacetimes.

# Abstract

We investigate the interplay between Euclidean and Lorentzian formulations of interacting scalar field theories on curved backgrounds possessing continuous isometries, with particular emphasis on the analytic continuation between static Riemannian manifolds and their Lorentzian counterparts. Beginning with a scalar field theory formulated on a static Riemannian manifold, we examine how the isometry group of the Euclidean section constrains and determines the symmetry structure of the corresponding Lorentzian theory obtained via Wick rotation. Particular attention is paid to the subtleties arising when the Euclidean isometry group does not straightforwardly complexify to the full Lorentzian isometry group, and we clarify the conditions under which reflection positivity and the Osterwalder-Schrader reconstruction theorem extend to these more general curved settings. As a concrete and physically motivated example, we analyze the case of hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^d$ and its Lorentzian continuation to Anti-de Sitter space $\mathrm{AdS}_d$, tracing the fate of the $SO(d,1)$ isometry group of Euclidean $\mathbb{H}^d$ under continuation to the conformal group $SO(d-1,2)$ acting on Lorentzian $\mathrm{AdS}_d$. We show how interacting scalar correlation functions, constructed perturbatively in the Euclidean regime, continue to well-defined Wightman functions satisfying the appropriate Lorentzian commutation relations and causal structure. The construction highlights the role of the conformal boundary and global versus local isometries in mediating between the two signatures, and we discuss implications for bulk reconstruction and the AdS/CFT correspondence. Our results provide a systematic framework for extending Euclidean field-theoretic techniques to a broad class of curved Lorentzian spacetimes with sufficient symmetry, and clarify the precise sense in which space-time symmetries of interacting theories survive the transition between signatures.

We investigate the quantization of isometry generators on Riemannian symmetric spaces and their analytic continuation to pseudo-Riemannian spacetimes, focusing on the interplay between self-adjoint and unitary representations of the underlying symmetry algebra. Starting from hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^n$, whose isometry group $SO(n,1)$ acts via self-adjoint generators on $L^2(\mathbb{H}^n)$, we examine how analytic continuation in the curvature radius and signature transforms this structure into the unitary representation theory of $SO(n,2)$ acting on fields propagating on Anti-de Sitter space $AdS_{n+1}$. We show that the naive continuation of self-adjoint generators does not automatically yield unitary operators on the continued Hilbert space; rather, the reality properties of the generators, the choice of inner product, and the boundary conditions at the conformal boundary must be continued in tandem to preserve unitarity. We construct the explicit dictionary between the discrete/continuous spectral decomposition of the Laplacian on $\mathbb{H}^n$ and the principal/discrete series representations relevant to AdS, clarifying how normalizable and non-normalizable modes reorganize under the continuation. Particular attention is paid to the fate of the generator of "radial" translations, whose self-adjoint extension on the Euclidean space becomes, after continuation, a generator of time translations subject to the usual subtleties of choosing a unitary time evolution in a Lorentzian signature (energy positivity, choice of vacuum, and boundary unitarity). We illustrate the general formalism with the basic representations relevant for scalar fields, showing how the Euclidean self-adjoint Casimir spectrum matches the conformal weights $\Delta$ of unitary AdS/CFT representations, and we discuss the obstruction encountered when the continued spectrum fails to satisfy the unitarity bounds. # Summary

This research result establishes a correspondence between the classical theory of one-parameter isometry groups on static Riemannian manifolds and their quantum mechanical realizations, with an application to Lorentzian quantum field theory via Wick rotation.

**Core Result:** Given a static Riemannian manifold equipped with a one-parameter group of isometries, the associated infinitesimal generator admits a canonical quantization that bifurcates into two distinct operator-theoretic realizations:

1. **Self-adjoint quantization** — corresponding to generators of *symmetric* flows, yielding one-parameter groups of unitary operators $e^{itH}$ on the Hilbert space of states, with $H$ self-adjoint by Stone's theorem.

2. **Unitary (or skew-adjoint) quantization** — corresponding to generators of *rotational/compact* isometries, producing genuinely unitary one-parameter subgroups without the need for analytic continuation, reflecting the geometric periodicity or boundedness of the underlying orbits.

The splitting arises naturally from the spectral decomposition of the isometry generator relative to the static structure (i.e., the existence of a global timelike Killing field defining the "static" character of the metric), which separates the tangent space of symmetries into components tangent to time-translations versus spatial rotations/boundedness.

**Wick Rotation and Lorentzian Representations:** Upon analytic continuation (Wick rotation) of the time parameter $t \mapsto it$, the Euclidean/Riemannian one-parameter subgroups extend to representations of the corresponding Lorentzian isometry group. The key finding is that:

- The self-adjoint generators in Riemannian signature become generators of *unitary* one-parameter groups in Lorentzian signature (via $e^{itH} \to e^{-tH}$ analytically continued back to unitary evolution), consistent with the reflection positivity mechanism familiar from Euclidean QFT (Osterwalder–Schwarter reconstruction).

- The already-unitary Riemannian subgroups persist as unitary representations after Wick rotation, since their generators are essentially skew-adjoint and their exponentials remain well-defined and unitary independent of the signature, reflecting that compact/rotational symmetries are insensitive to the choice of time signature.

**Significance:** This shows that the full isometry group of the static Riemannian manifold, upon quantization, produces a *unitary representation of the Lorentzian isometry group* after continuation, providing a rigorous bridge between Euclidean path-integral constructions and Lorentzian unitary quantum theories. This offers a structural explanation—rooted in the self-adjoint/unitary dichotomy of generators—for why Wick rotation of well-defined Euclidean QFTs yields consistent unitary Lorentzian theories, generalizing the Osterwalder-Schrader framework to a broader geometric setting involving arbitrary static isometry groups (not only time-translations).

We investigate the construction of unitary representations of Lorentzian isometry groups arising from Euclidean quantum field theories defined on static Riemannian manifolds. Starting from a Euclidean path integral formulation on a static manifold $M_E$ with isometry group $G_E$, we develop a systematic framework for analytically continuing correlation functions to obtain unitary representations of the Lorentzian isometry group $G_L$ acting on the physical Hilbert space of the continued theory. The construction relies on reflection positivity with respect to a chosen Euclidean time-slicing, which guarantees the existence of a well-defined Hilbert space inner product, together with an analysis of the complexification of the isometry algebra that identifies the subgroup of transformations admitting a unitary implementation after Wick rotation. We show that generators of Euclidean time translations and spatial isometries combine, under analytic continuation, into the generators of Lorentzian boosts and time translations, with the self-adjointness of the Lorentzian Hamiltonian following from the positivity properties of the Euclidean two-point functions.

We verify reflection positivity of the hyperbolic two-point function and demonstrate how bulk unitarity in global AdS coordinates follows directly from Euclidean correlator positivity, without recourse to holographic boundary data.
